content.text: Goals
Replace the current team wiki platform with PlexiiWrite to improve content accessibility, collaboration, and version control.
Enhance real-time editing capabilities and reduce time spent on manual documentation updates.
Ensure all existing knowledge base content is fully migrated with minimal data loss or formatting issues.
Improve searchability, mobile access, and user engagement across teams.
Scope
Include migration of all active and archived wiki pages (excluding external links or third-party resources).
Set up user roles, permissions, and access controls in alignment with current team structure.
Configure templates, workflows, and tagging systems to support structured documentation.
Provide training sessions for key stakeholders and regular users.
Deliver a phased rollout over two months, starting with core engineering and product teams.
Timeline
Week 1–2

data.title: Onboarding Guide for New Support Agent – First Week

content.text: Welcome and Overview

Welcome to the support team! This guide is designed to help you get up to speed during your first week. You’ll learn about key tools, standard processes, and how escalations are managed so you can provide consistent, efficient, and customer-focused support from day one.

Your first week will focus on understanding our systems, policies, and workflows. By the end of the week, you should be comfortable logging tickets, accessing knowledge bases, and recognizing when a case requires escalation.
Day 1: Orientation and Team Introduction
Attend the onboarding meeting with the Support Manager and Operations Lead.
Meet your team members: pair up with a buddy (a senior agent) for mentorship.
Review the company’s support philosophy and core values (e.g., empathy, speed, accuracy).
Receive access to internal tools and your user account.
Complete the new agent checklist (signed off by manager).
Key Takeaway
: You are not expected to solve every issue alone. Your role is to listen, respond, and escalate appropriately—ensuring customers feel heard and supported.
Day 2: Tools and Systems Setup
Key Tools You Will Use
Support Ticketing System (Zendesk)
Log all customer interactions.
Assign tickets, track status, and respond with clear, structured notes.
Use tags for categories (e.g., billing, technical, account access).
Set up auto-replies for common queries (e.g., “We’re reviewing your request”).
Knowledge Base (Confluence)
Search for answers to common issues using keywords.
Always verify information before sharing it with a customer.
Flag outdated or missing content to the knowledge team.
CRM (Salesforce)
Link tickets to customer records.
Update customer history and notes in real time.
Use the “Customer Journey” view to track interactions over time.
Internal Communication (Slack)
Join channels: #support-general, #onboarding, #escalations, #team-buddy.
Use @mentions to alert team members when needed.
Never share sensitive customer data in public channels.
Tip
: Bookmark the tools in your browser for quick access. Use keyboard shortcuts where available (e.g., Ctrl+T to open new tab in Zendesk).
Day 3: Standard Processes and Response Guidelines
Learn the standard response templates for common issues:
Billing inquiries
Login errors
Account access requests
Understand our SLA (Service Level Agreement):
First response within 15 minutes for urgent cases.
Resolution target of 24 hours for non-critical issues.
Practice writing clear, concise, and empathetic responses using the
STAR method
(Situation, Task, Action, Result) when documenting solutions.
Note
: Always confirm customer intent before offering a solution—avoid assumptions.
Day 4: Escalation Procedures
When to Escalate
Escalate if any of the following apply:
Customer is clearly frustrated or emotionally charged.
The issue requires technical expertise beyond your scope (e.g., server errors, network issues).
No resolution found after two attempts with standard solutions.
The issue involves financial risk or compliance concerns (e.g., data breach, unauthorized access).
How to Escalate
Identify the Need
Clearly state the problem in the ticket notes.
Include relevant logs, screenshots, or error messages.
Use the Escalation Path
In Zendesk, click “Escalate” → select “Technical Team” or “Product Support.”
Add a note:
“Customer is experiencing [issue], has tried [steps], no resolution. Requesting immediate review.”
Notify Your Buddy or Manager
Send a brief Slack message to your buddy or manager:
“Ticket #12345 escalated due to [reason]. Customer name: [Name]. Please advise if further action is needed.”
Follow Up
Check back in 15 minutes to confirm status.
Update the customer with a timeline (e.g., “We’ve escalated this to our engineering team and will follow up by 3 PM”).
Escalation Timeframes
Tier 1 (Agent): 24 hours max for resolution.
Tier 2 (Escalated): Response within 1 hour of escalation.
Day 5: Review, Feedback, and Next Steps
Attend a short review meeting with your manager and buddy.
Go over three sample tickets you handled during the week.
Discuss any confusion or questions about tools or processes.
Complete the onboarding feedback form.
Receive your first performance score and next training assignment (e.g., advanced troubleshooting or compliance modules).
Next Week
: Focus on handling more complex cases and shadowing a senior agent during live support sessions.
Final Notes
You are here because you care about customer experience. Your job is not just to fix problems—it’s to build trust through consistency, clarity, and compassion.
Always double-check:
Customer identity and data privacy
Accuracy of solutions
Escalation timing and documentation
If something feels off—pause, verify, and escalate. You’re not alone in this.
Welcome to the team. We’re excited to have you!
— Support Onboarding Team [Date: [launch date]] [Owner Name: [manager name]]

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: Why Bug Reports Matter
bullets: Clear bug reports help developers fix issues faster
Reduce back-and-forth communication between teams
Improve product quality and user satisfaction
Ensure consistent understanding of what’s broken
Save time by avoiding guesswork and retesting
Build trust through transparency and precision
slides.notes: Start with the importance of clarity. Emphasize that a good report isn’t just about describing a problem—it’s about enabling fast, accurate fixes. This saves everyone time and reduces frustration in the development cycle.

slides.title: The Core Elements of a Good Report
bullets: Describe the exact steps to reproduce the bug
Include the expected vs. actual behavior
Specify the environment (device, OS, browser, version)
State if the issue is reproducible or intermittent
Attach screenshots or logs when possible
Mention any error messages or stack traces
slides.notes: These elements form the foundation of a useful bug report. Walk through each one briefly and explain why it’s necessary—like how environment details help developers know if the issue is isolated or widespread.

slides.title: How to Reproduce It Step by Step
bullets: Start with a clear, numbered sequence of actions
Ensure steps are simple and repeatable
Include user context (e.g., logged in, on homepage)
Stop at the point where the bug appears
Verify that the same steps always trigger the issue
slides.notes: Reproducibility is key. Stress that users should not just describe what happened—they must show exactly how to get there. This helps developers verify and fix without needing extra questions.

slides.title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls
bullets: Never say 'it’s broken'—be specific about what breaks
Skip vague statements like 'something isn’t working'
Don’t assume the developer knows your environment
Avoid emotional language or blame
Don’t include personal opinions or guesses
slides.notes: Common mistakes come from lack of precision. Remind everyone that a good report is neutral, factual, and focused on facts—not feelings or assumptions. Use examples to show how vague reports fail.

slides.title: Example: From Vague to Clear
bullets: Vague: 'The app crashes sometimes.'
Clear: 'After clicking 'Save' on the profile page, the app crashes on iOS 16 with Safari, version 2.3.1.'
Added: Steps, environment, expected behavior, reproducibility
slides.notes: Show a real-world example side by side. This illustrates the transformation from unhelpful to actionable. It makes the difference tangible and easy to recognize in practice.

slides.title: Next Steps & Best Practices
bullets: Always use a standardized bug report template
Submit reports through the team’s tracking tool (e.g., Jira or Bugzilla)
Follow up if the issue isn’t resolved within 24 hours
Encourage team members to review and validate reports before submission
slides.notes: Wrap up with actionable takeaways. Reinforce that consistency and process matter. Encourage everyone to adopt the template and check each other’s reports for completeness.

# Performance and Memory Analysis — Widgets and Browsers

Grounded in the current code. Numbers are engineering estimates from the architecture, not measured profiles; the last section says how to measure them for real. The headline: browsers dominate memory, the canvas has no offscreen culling, and live wires are the main CPU hot path during interaction.

## 1. The model that decides everything

Three architectural facts drive every number below.

Only the active desk is mounted. `loadForTask` wipes the widget store and loads just the open task's widgets, so widgets on other desks cost nothing while you are not on them. Portals are the exception and they are cheap (see below). So "how many widgets hurt" is really "how many on ONE desk."

No viewport culling. `Canvas.tsx` renders `widgets.map((w) => renderWidget(w))` with no check for whether a widget is in view. Every widget on the active desk is fully mounted and live whether it is on screen, panned far away, or hidden behind another widget. Section children render too. There is no virtualization.

Each browser is a real Chromium process that never sleeps. `webviewTag: true`, `sandbox: false`, each `<webview>` gets its own session partition, and there is no `backgroundThrottling`, no `visibilitychange` handling, and no IntersectionObserver in `WebViewWidget`. So an offscreen or hidden browser still runs its timers, animations, video, and JavaScript at full cost. This is the single biggest stability lever in the app.

## 2. Per-widget cost

Memory is per live widget on the active desk. CPU-at-rest is the steady cost when you are not touching it.

| Widget | Est. RAM each | CPU at rest | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| webview (browser) | 80 MB light page, 150-400 MB for SPAs (Gmail, Notion, Figma, image-heavy marketing) | Medium-High; full when offscreen | Separate Chromium renderer process + the live page. No throttling. |
| local-app-launcher (mirror mode) | Native app + a capture/composite cost | Medium | Punch-through of a real native window. |
| diagram | 10-30 MB | Low-Medium | React Flow (`@xyflow/react`) is a heavy graph runtime. |
| page / markdown | 5-15 MB | Low | Full Tiptap / ProseMirror editor instance each. |
| scratchpad | 5-20 MB (grows with strokes) | Low | Canvas + perfect-freehand stroke buffers. |
| streamdeck | 3-8 MB | Low | 10x3 button grid + media/app bindings. |
| table | 2-10 MB (rows) | Low | Rows + per-cell field editors. |
| mindmap | 2-8 MB | Low | Node tree + SVG. |
| voice-recorder | small idle, large while recording | High while recording | MediaRecorder + audio buffers. |
| video / image / file | size of the media | Low-Medium | Decoded media in memory; video keeps decoding. |
| agent | 1-3 MB | Low; spikes on run | Config + run log; AI cost on each run, browser-driving cost if wired to a browser. |
| portal | 1-2 MB | Low (4s poll) | Renders a static `DeskMiniature` of another desk from a `listByTask` poll every 4s. It does NOT mount that desk's live webviews, so a control room of portals is cheap. |
| minimap | small RAM, notable CPU on re-render | Medium on change | Auto-created per desk; renders EVERY widget as a scaled live `WidgetPreview` in a foreignObject, so its re-render cost scales with widget count. |
| sticky / note / card / shape / field / calculator / color / timer / task-link | 0.2-1 MB | Negligible | DOM + React only. |

Baseline before any widgets: the main process, the GPU process, and the React renderer window together are roughly 250-450 MB.

## 3. The CPU hot paths (scale with count, not just memory)

Live wires overlay. `LinkOverlay` rebuilds its segments by calling `getBoundingClientRect` (via `querySelector` on `data-widget-id`) for BOTH endpoints of EVERY wire on every render, and it runs a `requestAnimationFrame` loop that re-renders every frame while the mouse is held. So during a drag the cost is O(wires) DOM reads per frame. With a few wires this is invisible; with 30-50+ wires and an active drag it starts dropping frames. Firing wires add SMIL animations on top, which are cheap individually but add up.

Minimap re-render. The minimap subscribes to widget/pan/zoom/layout changes and re-renders every widget as a live preview. On a desk with many widgets, every layout change re-runs that whole render. It is the second hot path after wires.

No culling means mount cost is total, not visible. Panning a huge desk keeps all editors, canvases, and especially browsers alive and compositing. The compositor has to manage every webview layer even when off screen, which is where pan/zoom jank comes from on browser-heavy desks.

Background timers (app-wide, independent of widget count): body-double presence ~30s, time-of-day tint ~1 min, plus the inbox poller, drift detector, hyperfocus guardian, focus-session ticker, and the sync indicator. None are per-widget; together they are a small, constant background load. Per-widget timers exist for interval-trigger agents and the 4s portal poll.

## 4. Risk thresholds

Browsers on one desk:
- 1-3: comfortable. Roughly 0.5-1.2 GB total. Fine everywhere.
- 4-8: 1.2-3 GB. Fine on 16 GB Macs; noticeable on 8 GB, some swap.
- 9-15: 3-6 GB, real swap pressure on 8-16 GB machines, pan/zoom jank as the compositor juggles many webview layers. Heavy SPAs (Gmail, Figma, Notion) hit the top of this range fast.
- 16+: high risk. Multi-GB swap, beachballs, and on lower-RAM machines the OS can start killing renderer processes (a browser widget goes blank). This is the most likely path to instability today.

Non-browser widgets on one desk:
- up to ~30: no perceptible cost.
- 30-60: fine at rest; drag/pan with many wires begins to show frame drops, and minimap re-renders get heavier.
- 60-120: input latency on pan/drag becomes noticeable, especially with editors (page/markdown), a diagram, or 40+ wires in play.
- 120+: sluggish even at rest from React reconciliation and the no-cull mount cost; this is well beyond normal use but reachable on a "dump everything" desk.

Wires specifically: under ~20 are free; 30-50 start to matter during drag; 80+ make dragging visibly choppy because of the per-frame O(wires) bound reads.

Live agents: not a memory cliff but a CPU and cost one. Several interval agents, or an agent driving a browser in a tool loop, add steady CPU and real API spend. The risk is runaway cost and a busy browser, not RAM.

## 5. Stability risks, ranked

1. Browser-process memory exhaustion. The clearest failure mode. Many webviews, especially heavy SPAs, can exhaust RAM and trigger OS-level renderer kills (blank browser widgets) or heavy swap. No suspension of offscreen browsers makes this worse than it needs to be.
2. Compositor jank on browser-heavy desks. Even within memory limits, many live webview layers make pan/zoom stutter because nothing is culled.
3. Drag-time wire cost. O(wires) bound reads per animation frame during drags on wire-dense desks.
4. Agent browser-driving and intervals. CPU and API cost, plus an agent navigating a shared browser the user is also using.
5. Minimap re-render cost on very dense desks.

## 6. Recommendations, prioritized

The first two remove most of the risk for the least work.

P1. Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers. Add an IntersectionObserver (or a pan/zoom-driven visibility check) in `WebViewWidget`; when a browser is fully off screen or fully occluded, stop it doing work: mute audio, and ideally detach or freeze it. Electron can `webContents.setBackgroundThrottling`, and a stronger move is to unload the `<webview>` when far offscreen and reload its URL when it returns. This directly attacks risk 1 and 2.

P2. Viewport-cull the canvas. In `Canvas.tsx`, skip mounting widgets whose bounds are well outside the viewport (with a margin), so a giant desk only mounts what is near view. Browsers benefit most. This attacks risk 2 and 5 and the no-cull mount cost generally.

P3. Soft-cap and warn on browsers per desk. Track live webview count and, past a threshold (say 8), surface a gentle "this desk has many browsers, performance may drop" hint rather than a hard limit. Cheap, prevents the worst surprises.

P4. Throttle the wire overlay. Cap the `LinkOverlay` rAF to ~30fps during drag, cache bound reads within a frame, and skip wires whose endpoints are offscreen.

P5. Throttle the minimap. Debounce its re-render and render simple rectangles instead of full `WidgetPreview` previews above a widget-count threshold.

P6. Lazy-mount heavy widgets. Defer mounting Tiptap/React Flow/scratchpad until the widget is near the viewport (a lighter version of P2 scoped to editors).

P7. A dev performance overlay. Surface `app.getAppMetrics()` (per-process memory and CPU) and a live widget/webview/wire count so this analysis can be replaced with real numbers and regressions caught.

## 7. How to measure for real

- `app.getAppMetrics()` in main returns per-process type, PID, CPU, and memory. Log it on an interval, or expose it in the dev overlay (P7). This is the single most useful instrument; it shows exactly how much each browser process costs.
- macOS Activity Monitor, filter for the app: you will see one row per webview renderer process. Open desks with 1, then 5, then 10 browsers and watch the total.
- Chrome DevTools Performance panel on the renderer window during a pan/drag on a wire-dense desk shows the `LinkOverlay` and minimap costs directly.
- `chrome://tracing` style frame profiling confirms compositor jank on browser-heavy desks.

Replace the estimates in sections 2-4 with measured values once P7 exists.

---

**Key Findings:**

1. Browsers dominate memory usage due to full Chromium processes running even when offscreen or hidden.
2. No viewport culling means every widget on the active desk is fully mounted and rendered, leading to high memory and CPU costs, especially with many widgets or browsers.
3. Live wires create a significant CPU hot path during drag operations (O(wires) DOM reads per frame), causing noticeable frame drops with 30+ wires.
4. Minimap re-renders scale with widget count, becoming expensive on dense desks.
5. Background timers contribute a small but constant load; per-widget timers add up for agents and portals.
6. Memory pressure from browsers is the primary stability risk, with thresholds clearly defined: 1–3 browsers are safe, 4–8 cause noticeable strain, and 9+ risk OS-level instability.

**Top 3 Recommendations:**

1. **Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers** – Implement IntersectionObserver or pan/zoom visibility checks to pause browser activity when off-screen, reducing memory and CPU load and preventing OS-level renderer kills.

2. **Viewport-cull the canvas** – Skip rendering widgets outside the viewport (with margin) to reduce mount cost and compositor load, especially benefiting browser-heavy desks and minimizing pan/zoom jank.

3. **Soft-cap and warn on browsers per desk** – Track live webview count and provide a performance warning at 8+ browsers to prevent unexpected degradation without imposing hard limits.
